# From baseline to learning model {#sec-b05}

```{r}
#| label: setup-b05
#| include: false
source("../R/style.R")
set.seed(2605)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance
**Guiding question:** Which additional effort delivers an improvement that matters for a decision?

**For:** clinicians, doctoral researchers and reviewers who build or appraise a first prediction model ·
**Prerequisites:** @sec-b02 (prediction versus explanation), @sec-b03 (missing values and denominators), @sec-b04
(a reproducible R project)

**In the course:** [W1 · From clinical case to question](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w1-from-clinical-case-to-question.html)
and [W3 · Diagnostics, prediction and evidence](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w3-diagnostics-prediction-evidence.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in this chapter; teaching file `data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv`, reused in @sec-b06) ·
**Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b05-case}

The orthogeriatric team of a fictitious trauma department can offer proactive geriatric co-management to about 30 of
every 100 patients aged 65 or older who are admitted with a hip fracture. The aim is to prevent postoperative
delirium, an acute confusional state that prolongs recovery and is often missed. Today the ward uses a three-item
points rule. A colleague proposes a gradient-boosting model that draws on 19 routine variables from the hospital
information system. The head of the team has to decide which approach goes into a six-month pilot. The question is
not which method is more modern. It is whether the extra effort — a data feed, tuning, maintenance and explanation to
staff — finds more patients who will develop delirium within the same capacity. If the team chooses wrongly, either
geriatric time is spent on low-risk patients or preventable delirium goes unnoticed.

## Core reading {#sec-b05-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended for W1 and W3 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

A prediction model is a rule that turns information available at one point in time into an estimated risk for a
later event. The point in time matters. Here it is the first morning after admission. Everything the model uses must
be known by then, and the outcome — delirium within five days after surgery — must lie in the future. With this
framing fixed, the methods form a ladder. Each rung adds capacity to learn from data and adds effort.

**The ladder of candidates.** The *null model* predicts the same risk for everyone, namely the proportion of patients
with delirium in the development data. It cannot rank anybody, but it sets the floor: a model that does not beat it
has learned nothing useful. A *points rule* adds one point per risk factor, in our case age 85 or older, pre-existing
cognitive impairment and an anaesthetic risk class (ASA) of 3 or higher. Clinicians can apply it at the bedside.
*Logistic regression* estimates a weight for each of a small set of prespecified predictors and returns a probability
(details in [Methods in R: Logistic Regression](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-07-regression.html#sec-chapters-07-regression-logistic-regression)).
*Regularised regression* such as the elastic net offers the same model many more candidate predictors but shrinks
their weights towards zero and can drop some entirely [@zou2005elasticnet]; the amount of shrinkage is a tuning
parameter ([Methods in R: Elastic Net](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-07-regression.html#sec-chapters-07-regression-elastic-net)).
*Tree ensembles and boosting* build many small decision trees in sequence and can capture thresholds, curved
relationships and interactions without being told about them [@chen2016xgboost]. They have several tuning
parameters. The top rung, *representation learning* with neural networks, learns its own features from raw signals
such as images or spectra. It plays no part here because our data are 19 numbers per patient; @sec-b09 and @sec-b10
return to it.

Moving up the ladder does not guarantee better predictions. A systematic review of 71 studies found no average
performance benefit of machine learning over logistic regression among comparisons at low risk of bias; an advantage
for machine learning appeared only among comparisons at high risk of bias [@christodoulou2019mlvslr]. The useful
question is therefore not “which method wins?” but “which improvement survives a fair comparison and changes what
the team does?”

**Three places, three jobs.** A fair comparison needs to keep three jobs apart (@tbl-b05-steps). *Preprocessing* —
here the replacement of missing laboratory values by a median — is learned from development data only and then
applied unchanged to anybody else. *Tuning* — the choice of shrinkage for the elastic net and of the number of
boosting rounds — uses an inner cross-validation within the development data: the 800 development patients are
divided into five folds, each fold is predicted once by a model trained on the other four, and the setting with the
best average performance is kept ([Methods in R: Cross-Validation](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-cross-validation)).
The *independent test* uses 400 patients who were set aside before anything else happened and who are predicted
once, by every candidate, at the very end.

| Step | Data used | What happens | Do test patients take part? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Split | all 1,200 patients | random allocation of patient IDs: 800 development, 400 test | allocation only |
| Preprocessing | 800 development patients | medians for missing haemoglobin and sodium | no |
| Tuning | 800 development patients, 5 inner folds | shrinkage and mixing (elastic net), number of rounds (boosting) | no |
| Choice of family | inner cross-validation results | prespecified: regression unless a flexible model is better by ≥ 0.02 in AUC | no |
| Final fit | 800 development patients | each candidate refitted once with its chosen settings | no |
| Independent test | 400 test patients | one prediction per candidate, same patients for all | yes, once |

: Where each step of the lab takes place. Counts are *synthetic*. {#tbl-b05-steps}

The validation in this chapter is therefore exactly this: **a single random split into development and test data
(internal hold-out validation), with an inner five-fold cross-validation used only for tuning and for the choice of
model family.** It is not nested cross-validation, not temporal validation and not external validation. A nested
cross-validation would repeat the tuning inside each of several outer folds and so estimate the performance of the
whole procedure without a separate test set [@varma2006nestedcv]
([Methods in R: Nested Cross-Validation](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-13-ml.html#sec-chapters-13-ml-nested-cv)).
Temporal and external validation ask a different question — does the model hold in a later period or another
hospital? — and are the subject of @sec-b19.

```{r}
#| label: b05-core-compute
#| include: false
#| ref.label: [b05-generate, b05-split, b05-preprocess, b05-simple-candidates, b05-elastic-net, b05-boosting, b05-inner-cv, b05-test]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b05-auc
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Discrimination of five candidates on the same 400 synthetic test patients (103 with delirium). Points: area under the ROC curve (AUC); bars: 95% percentile bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples of patients). Labels: delirium cases among the 120 patients ranked highest (30% capacity). Unit: patient; data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Dot-and-interval chart with five rows, one per candidate model, showing the AUC on 400 test patients. ", paste0(res$model, ": AUC ", sprintf("%.2f", res$auc), ", ", res$found, " of ", sum(pred$y), " cases found among the 120 highest-ranked patients", collapse = "; "), ". The intervals of the rule, regression, elastic net and boosting overlap widely; the null model has no interval.")'
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| ref.label: b05-figure-code
```

Two observations follow from @fig-b05-auc, which is computed in the lab. First, all models beat the null model by a
wide margin, and the regression models rank patients somewhat better than the points rule. Second, the differences
between regression, elastic net and boosting are small compared with the width of the intervals. With 400 test
patients and about 100 events, an AUC difference of 0.02 cannot be distinguished from chance. The decision-relevant
reading is the label: within the capacity of 120 patients, the candidates find between `r min(res$found[-1])` and `r max(res$found[-1])` of `r sum(pred$y)` future
delirium cases. A handful of additional cases per 400 patients may matter — but only if the gain is real, holds in
the next year's patients, and is worth a data feed of 19 variables.

**The most important assumption of this comparison is that the 400 test patients come from the same hospital,
period and data-generating process as the development patients.** Under this assumption a random hold-out set
estimates how the model performs for similar patients; it says nothing about another hospital, a new protocol or next
winter's case mix.

A last point concerns honesty with the test set. If the team had compared ten models on the 400 test patients and
reported the best, the winning number would be optimistic, because the test set would have been used for selection.
In this chapter the choice of model family is fixed in advance and made on the inner cross-validation; the test set
only confirms it.

**Question for the workshop:** In the test set the elastic net finds a few more cases than the rule and the
regression, while boosting finds none more than the rule. Which
additional evidence would you need before you accept the cost of a 19-variable data feed — and which of these
questions could the hold-out test answer at all?

## Lab {#sec-b05-lab}

The lab runs in a fresh R session in well under a minute. It generates the cohort, splits it once, learns the
preprocessing, tunes two models in the inner folds, compares all five candidates on the inner folds and finally
predicts the test patients once.

### Step 1 · Generate the synthetic cohort

Every value below is *synthetic*. The coefficients in the data-generating model are teaching *assumptions*, chosen
to be clinically plausible in direction; they are not estimates from any study. Because the data are simulated we
also know each patient's true risk, which no real data set contains. We keep it for the counter-check in @sec-b06.

```{r}
#| label: b05-generate
set.seed(2605)                                          # fixed start value for the whole lab
n <- 1200
id <- sprintf("P%04d", seq_len(n))                      # constant patient IDs, reused in B06

# Eight clinically motivated predictors
age <- pmin(101, 65 + round(rgamma(n, shape = 3.5, scale = 5)))           # years
cognitive_impairment <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3.0 + 0.09 * (age - 65)))   # pre-existing, 0/1
asa <- as.integer(cut(rnorm(n, 0.03 * (age - 80), 1),                   # ASA class 1-4
                      c(-Inf, -1.7, 0, 1.25, Inf)))
haemoglobin <- round(rnorm(n, 12.0 - 0.02 * (age - 80), 1.6), 1)          # g/dL
sodium <- round(rnorm(n, 138.5, 4))                                       # mmol/L
n_medications <- rpois(n, 3 + 0.08 * (age - 65))                          # regular medicines
hours_to_surgery <- round(rgamma(n, shape = 2, scale = 14))               # hours from admission
sensory_impairment <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)                                   # vision or hearing, 0/1

# Eleven further routine variables; only CRP and albumin carry a weak signal
potassium <- round(rnorm(n, 4.2, 0.5), 1)        # mmol/L
creatinine <- round(rlnorm(n, log(1.0), 0.3), 2) # mg/dL
crp <- round(rlnorm(n, log(15), 1), 0)           # mg/L
leukocytes <- round(rlnorm(n, log(9), 0.3), 1)   # 10^9/L
glucose <- round(rlnorm(n, log(120), 0.25))      # mg/dL
albumin <- round(rnorm(n, 36, 5))                # g/L
bmi <- round(rnorm(n, 24, 4), 1)                 # kg/m^2
heart_rate <- round(rnorm(n, 85, 14))            # beats/min
systolic_bp <- round(rnorm(n, 140, 22))          # mmHg
temperature <- round(rnorm(n, 36.9, 0.4), 1)     # degrees C
spo2 <- pmin(100, round(rnorm(n, 95, 2.5)))      # %

# True linear predictor (assumption): includes a U-shaped sodium effect that no linear term captures
lp <- -1.6 + 0.065 * (age - 80) + 1.1 * cognitive_impairment + 0.35 * (asa - 2.7) -
  0.18 * (haemoglobin - 12) + 0.012 * ((sodium - 139)^2 - 16) + 0.09 * (n_medications - 4.5) +
  0.012 * (hours_to_surgery - 28) + 0.35 * sensory_impairment + 0.004 * (crp - 25) - 0.03 * (albumin - 36)
true_risk <- plogis(lp)
delirium <- rbinom(n, 1, true_risk)              # postoperative delirium within 5 days, 0/1

# Missing laboratory values (assumption: missing completely at random, see B03)
haemoglobin[sample(n, 70)] <- NA
sodium[sample(n, 45)] <- NA

cohort <- data.frame(id, age, cognitive_impairment, asa, haemoglobin, sodium, n_medications,
                     hours_to_surgery, sensory_impairment, potassium, creatinine, crp, leukocytes,
                     glucose, albumin, bmi, heart_rate, systolic_bp, temperature, spo2,
                     true_risk = round(true_risk, 4), delirium)
stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == 1200, !anyDuplicated(cohort$id), sum(cohort$delirium) == 320)
```

The cohort has `r cdsr_number(nrow(cohort))` patients, `r sum(cohort$delirium)` of whom develop delirium
(`r cdsr_percent(mean(cohort$delirium))`).

### Step 2 · Split once, by patient, and assign the inner folds

The split is made on patient IDs before any model sees the data. Each patient has one admission here; with repeated
admissions the split would have to be made on the person, not the admission (@sec-b19).

```{r}
#| label: b05-split
test_ids <- sort(sample(cohort$id, 400))                        # independent test patients
cohort$split <- ifelse(cohort$id %in% test_ids, "test", "development")
dev_ids <- cohort$id[cohort$split == "development"]
inner_fold <- setNames(sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(dev_ids))), dev_ids)
cohort$fold <- ifelse(cohort$split == "development", inner_fold[cohort$id], NA)  # 1-5; NA for test

dev <- cohort[cohort$split == "development", ]
test <- cohort[cohort$split == "test", ]
stopifnot(length(intersect(dev$id, test$id)) == 0,              # no patient in both sets
          nrow(dev) == 800, nrow(test) == 400,
          sum(dev$delirium) == 217, sum(test$delirium) == 103,
          all(table(dev$fold) == 160))
table(set = cohort$split, delirium = cohort$delirium)
```

### Step 3 · Learn the preprocessing from development data only

```{r}
#| label: b05-preprocess
core <- c("age", "cognitive_impairment", "asa", "haemoglobin", "sodium", "n_medications",
          "hours_to_surgery", "sensory_impairment")
extra <- c("potassium", "creatinine", "crp", "leukocytes", "glucose", "albumin", "bmi",
           "heart_rate", "systolic_bp", "temperature", "spo2")
all_pred <- c(core, extra)

medians <- sapply(dev[all_pred], median, na.rm = TRUE)          # learned on development data
impute <- function(d, m) {                                      # applies stored medians, learns nothing
  for (v in names(m)) d[[v]][is.na(d[[v]])] <- m[[v]]
  d
}
dev_i <- impute(dev, medians)
test_i <- impute(test, medians)
stopifnot(!anyNA(dev_i[all_pred]), !anyNA(test_i[all_pred]))
medians[c("haemoglobin", "sodium")]
```

One simplification is deliberate and must be stated: the medians come from all 800 development patients, so inside
the inner cross-validation the held-out fold has contributed a little to its own imputation. For a median this
effect is negligible; for steps that learn more from the data, such as selecting predictors, it is not (see the box
“Common mistake” below). A pipeline that refits every preprocessing step within each fold removes the issue.

### Step 4 · Null model, points rule and logistic regression

```{r}
#| label: b05-simple-candidates
auc <- function(p, y) {                       # rank formula (Mann-Whitney), equals the ROC area
  r <- rank(p); n1 <- sum(y); n0 <- length(y) - n1
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
brier <- function(p, y) mean((p - y)^2)       # mean squared error of the predicted risk

rule_points <- function(d) (d$age >= 85) + d$cognitive_impairment + (d$asa >= 3)   # 0-3 points
fit_rule <- function(d) tapply(d$delirium, factor(rule_points(d), levels = 0:3), mean)
predict_rule <- function(tab, d) as.numeric(tab[as.character(rule_points(d))])

f_lr <- reformulate(core, response = "delirium")                # eight prespecified predictors, linear
fit_rule(dev_i)                                                 # observed risk per point (development)
```

### Step 5 · Elastic net, tuned in the inner folds

`cv.glmnet()` [@friedman2010glmnet] runs the inner cross-validation for a sequence of shrinkage values λ. We pass our
own fold vector so that every candidate sees the same folds, and repeat it for five values of the mixing parameter α
(0 = ridge, 1 = lasso). The combination with the lowest cross-validated deviance is kept.

```{r}
#| label: b05-elastic-net
library(glmnet)
x_dev <- as.matrix(dev_i[all_pred]); x_test <- as.matrix(test_i[all_pred])
alphas <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
cv_fits <- lapply(alphas, function(a)
  cv.glmnet(x_dev, dev_i$delirium, family = "binomial", alpha = a,
            foldid = dev_i$fold, keep = TRUE))                    # keep = out-of-fold predictions
best <- which.min(sapply(cv_fits, function(cv) min(cv$cvm)))
en_cv <- cv_fits[[best]]
en_alpha <- alphas[best]; en_lambda <- en_cv$lambda.min
en_coef <- coef(en_cv, s = "lambda.min")
en_nonzero <- sum(en_coef[-1, 1] != 0)                          # predictors kept by the elastic net
c(alpha = en_alpha, lambda = round(en_lambda, 4), predictors_kept = en_nonzero)
```

### Step 6 · Gradient boosting, tuned in the inner folds

Depth, learning rate and minimum leaf size are fixed in advance; only the number of boosting rounds is tuned, with
early stopping on the same five folds. With one thread and no subsampling the result is reproducible.

```{r}
#| label: b05-boosting
library(xgboost)
xgb_params <- list(objective = "binary:logistic", max_depth = 2, eta = 0.05,
                   min_child_weight = 5, eval_metric = "logloss", nthread = 1)
fold_index <- lapply(1:5, function(f) which(dev_i$fold == f))
xgb_cv <- xgb.cv(params = xgb_params, data = xgb.DMatrix(x_dev, label = dev_i$delirium),
                 nrounds = 1000, folds = fold_index, early_stopping_rounds = 30, verbose = 0)
xgb_rounds <- xgb_cv$early_stop$best_iteration
xgb_rounds
```

### Step 7 · Compare all candidates on the inner folds

All five candidates are now evaluated on the same inner folds of the development data. AUC and Brier score are
computed per fold and averaged, so that the null model receives its correct AUC of 0.5. The test patients are still
untouched.

```{r}
#| label: b05-inner-cv
oof <- data.frame(id = dev_i$id, fold = dev_i$fold, y = dev_i$delirium,
                  null = NA, rule = NA, lr = NA, en = NA, xgb = NA)
for (f in 1:5) {
  tr <- dev_i$fold != f; ho <- dev_i$fold == f                  # training folds and held-out fold
  oof$null[ho] <- mean(dev_i$delirium[tr])
  oof$rule[ho] <- predict_rule(fit_rule(dev_i[tr, ]), dev_i[ho, ])
  oof$lr[ho] <- predict(glm(f_lr, binomial, dev_i[tr, ]), dev_i[ho, ], type = "response")
  booster <- xgb.train(params = xgb_params, nrounds = xgb_rounds, verbose = 0,
                       data = xgb.DMatrix(x_dev[tr, ], label = dev_i$delirium[tr]))
  oof$xgb[ho] <- predict(booster, xgb.DMatrix(x_dev[ho, ]))
}
oof$en <- plogis(en_cv$fit.preval[, en_cv$index["min", 1]])     # out-of-fold, at the chosen lambda

models <- c(null = "Null model", rule = "Points rule", lr = "Logistic regression",
            en = "Elastic net", xgb = "Gradient boosting")
fold_mean <- function(metric, m) mean(sapply(1:5, function(f) {
  s <- oof$fold == f; metric(oof[[m]][s], oof$y[s]) }))
inner <- data.frame(model = models,
                    auc = sapply(names(models), function(m) fold_mean(auc, m)),
                    brier = sapply(names(models), function(m) fold_mean(brier, m)))
inner$auc[1] <- 0.5                                             # constant prediction: exactly 0.5
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fold_mean(auc, "null"), 0.5)))

# Prespecified choice of family: regression unless a flexible model is better by >= 0.02 AUC
gain_flex <- max(inner["en", "auc"], inner["xgb", "auc"]) - inner["lr", "auc"]
chosen <- if (gain_flex >= 0.02) "flexible model" else "logistic regression"
knitr::kable(inner, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Candidate", "AUC (inner CV)", "Brier score (inner CV)"),
             caption = "Inner five-fold cross-validation on 800 synthetic development patients (217 with delirium); metrics averaged over folds.")
```

On the development data the best flexible model differs from logistic regression by
`r sprintf("%+.3f", gain_flex)` in AUC, so the prespecified criterion selects **`r chosen`**. The cross-validated
values of the two tuned models are slightly optimistic, because the same folds served for tuning and for this
comparison; nested cross-validation would remove that optimism.

### Step 8 · Final fits and one look at the test set

```{r}
#| label: b05-test
lr_fit <- glm(f_lr, binomial, dev_i)
booster <- xgb.train(params = xgb_params, nrounds = xgb_rounds, verbose = 0,
                     data = xgb.DMatrix(x_dev, label = dev_i$delirium))
pred <- data.frame(id = test_i$id, y = test_i$delirium,
                   null = mean(dev_i$delirium),
                   rule = predict_rule(fit_rule(dev_i), test_i),
                   lr = predict(lr_fit, test_i, type = "response"),
                   en = as.numeric(predict(en_cv, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "response")),
                   xgb = predict(booster, xgb.DMatrix(x_test)))
stopifnot(identical(pred$id, test$id))                          # same test patients for every candidate

# Paired bootstrap: resample test patients, recompute every AUC on the same resample
set.seed(5051)
boot <- replicate(2000, {
  i <- sample(nrow(pred), replace = TRUE)
  sapply(names(models)[-1], function(m) auc(pred[[m]][i], pred$y[i]))
})

# Decision-oriented reading: cases among the 120 highest-ranked patients (30% capacity).
# Ties (rule: four risk levels; null model: one) are broken in a fixed random order.
set.seed(5052)
tie_breaker <- runif(nrow(pred))
found_in_top <- function(p, y, k = 120) sum(y[order(-p, tie_breaker)[seq_len(k)]])

res <- data.frame(model = models,
                  auc = sapply(names(models), function(m) auc(pred[[m]], pred$y)),
                  lower = c(NA, apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.025)),
                  upper = c(NA, apply(boot, 1, quantile, 0.975)),
                  brier = sapply(names(models), function(m) brier(pred[[m]], pred$y)),
                  found = sapply(names(models), function(m) found_in_top(pred[[m]], pred$y)),
                  predictors = c(0, 3, length(core), en_nonzero, length(all_pred)))
res$auc[1] <- 0.5
diff_xgb_lr <- quantile(boot["xgb", ] - boot["lr", ], c(0.025, 0.975))
diff_en_lr <- quantile(boot["en", ] - boot["lr", ], c(0.025, 0.975))
stopifnot(abs(res["lr", "auc"] - 0.770) < 0.002, abs(res["rule", "auc"] - 0.730) < 0.002,
          abs(res["en", "auc"] - 0.781) < 0.003, abs(res["xgb", "auc"] - 0.742) < 0.01,
          res["lr", "found"] == 63, sum(pred$y) == 103)
knitr::kable(res, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Candidate", "AUC", "2.5%", "97.5%", "Brier score",
                           "Cases in top 120", "Predictors used"),
             caption = "Single evaluation on 400 synthetic test patients (103 with delirium). Interval: paired percentile bootstrap, 2,000 resamples of patients.")
```

The following code draws @fig-b05-auc in the core reading from the objects `res` and `pred`.

```{r}
#| label: b05-figure-code
#| eval: false
library(ggplot2)
plot_df <- res
plot_df$model <- factor(plot_df$model, levels = rev(models))
plot_df$label <- paste0(plot_df$found, " of ", sum(pred$y), " found")
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = auc, y = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = cdsr_linetypes[2], colour = cdsr_colours[["grey"]]) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), width = 0.2, orientation = "y",
                colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]], na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = model == "Null model"), size = 2.6, colour = cdsr_colours[["blue"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.86, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = "#333333") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = cdsr_shapes[1], `TRUE` = cdsr_shapes[3]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.45, 1.0), breaks = seq(0.5, 0.9, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "AUC on the test set (95% bootstrap interval)", y = NULL,
       caption = "n = 400 test patients, 103 events; synthetic data") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

The test results agree with the inner cross-validation in two respects: the regression ranks better than the rule,
and no flexible model is clearly better than the regression. Boosting tends to rank slightly worse: the paired
bootstrap interval for its AUC difference to the regression runs from `r sprintf("%.3f", diff_xgb_lr[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", diff_xgb_lr[2])`. The elastic net tends to rank slightly better, with an interval from
`r sprintf("%.3f", diff_en_lr[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", diff_en_lr[2])`. Both intervals reach zero, and in cases
found within the capacity the three models differ by at most `r max(res$found[3:5]) - min(res$found[3:5])` patients.
Brier scores — the mean squared distance between predicted risk and outcome — tell the same story.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
**Learning from the test patients before the test.** Typical forms are: choosing the ten predictors most strongly
associated with delirium on the full data set and then cross-validating; standardising or imputing with statistics of
all patients; trying several models on the test set and reporting the best. Each step lets information about the
held-out outcomes leak into the model, and the reported performance becomes optimistic. PROBAST+AI therefore asks
whether data leakage was avoided when data were split and whether all model development steps were repeated in each
resampling round [@moons2025probastai, model evaluation, signalling questions 4.5 and 4.6].
:::

### Step 9 · Export the teaching file

The cohort with its split and fold columns is written to `data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv`. @sec-b06 reads exactly this
file, so both chapters use identical patients and identical test IDs.

```{r}
#| label: b05-export
write.csv(cohort, "../data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv", row.names = FALSE)
check <- read.csv("../data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(check) == 1200, sum(check$split == "test") == 400,
          identical(sort(check$id[check$split == "test"]), test_ids))
```

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python/scikit-learn"}
**Original implementation.** scikit-learn [@pedregosa2011sklearn], stable release 1.9.1 (documentation checked
November 2026): [`Pipeline`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.html),
[`PredefinedSplit`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.PredefinedSplit.html),
[`GroupKFold`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold.html),
[`LogisticRegression`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression.html).

**Concrete advantage.** A `Pipeline` of imputer, scaler and model, tuned with `GridSearchCV`, refits the
preprocessing inside every inner fold and so removes the simplification of Step 3. `GroupKFold` keeps all admissions
of a patient in one fold.

**What must be identical.** The input file `data/b05-delirium-cohort.csv`, its split column and its inner folds
(imported with `PredefinedSplit(test_fold = fold - 1)`, not regenerated), the unit (patient), the metrics and an
agreed tolerance, for example ±0.005 in AUC. According to the scikit-learn user guide the penalty is divided by
n·C, so glmnet's λ corresponds to 1/(n·C) and α to `l1_ratio` [@friedman2010glmnet]; glmnet standardises
internally, scikit-learn only with a scaler in the pipeline. Elastic-net penalties need `solver = "saga"`, the
`penalty` argument is deprecated since version 1.8, and `LogisticRegression` is penalised by default (`C = 1.0`), so
the unpenalised `glm()` of Step 4 corresponds to `C = np.inf`.

**Status:** conceptual comparison, not executed. No statement about speed is made.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b05-countercheck}

**Change one thing: the size of the development data.** Keep the 400 test patients as they are, but develop the
regression, the elastic net (with the mixing parameter chosen above) and the boosting model on a random subset of
only 200 of the 800 development patients. Because a single subset is a single draw, repeat this 25 times.

*Before you run the code, write down your prediction:* Which candidate loses most discrimination? And in which
direction does the calibration slope of each model move? The calibration slope is the coefficient obtained when the
outcome is regressed on the logit of the predicted risk. A slope below 1 means that predictions are too extreme
(high risks too high, low risks too low), which is typical of overfitting; a slope above 1 means that they are too
cautious. @sec-b06 develops calibration in detail.

```{r}
#| label: b05-countercheck
cal_slope <- function(p, y) unname(coef(glm(y ~ qlogis(p), family = binomial))[2])
one_small_run <- function() {
  small <- dev_i[dev_i$id %in% sample(dev_i$id, 200), ]        # 200 patients, inner folds kept
  x_small <- as.matrix(small[all_pred])
  p_lr <- predict(glm(f_lr, binomial, small), test_i, type = "response")
  en_s <- cv.glmnet(x_small, small$delirium, family = "binomial", alpha = en_alpha, foldid = small$fold)
  p_en <- as.numeric(predict(en_s, newx = x_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
  xgb_s <- xgb.cv(params = xgb_params, data = xgb.DMatrix(x_small, label = small$delirium),
                  nrounds = 1000, folds = lapply(1:5, function(f) which(small$fold == f)),
                  early_stopping_rounds = 30, verbose = 0)
  p_xgb <- predict(xgb.train(params = xgb_params, verbose = 0, nrounds = xgb_s$early_stop$best_iteration,
                             data = xgb.DMatrix(x_small, label = small$delirium)), xgb.DMatrix(x_test))
  c(events = sum(small$delirium),
    auc_lr = auc(p_lr, pred$y), auc_en = auc(p_en, pred$y), auc_xgb = auc(p_xgb, pred$y),
    slope_lr = cal_slope(p_lr, pred$y), slope_en = cal_slope(p_en, pred$y),
    slope_xgb = cal_slope(p_xgb, pred$y))
}
set.seed(5053)
runs <- t(replicate(25, one_small_run()))                       # 25 subsets x 7 results
q <- function(v) quantile(v, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
counter <- data.frame(
  model = c("Logistic regression", "Elastic net", "Gradient boosting"),
  auc_800 = c(res["lr", "auc"], res["en", "auc"], res["xgb", "auc"]),
  auc_200 = sapply(c("auc_lr", "auc_en", "auc_xgb"), function(v) q(runs[, v])[2]),
  slope_800 = c(cal_slope(pred$lr, pred$y), cal_slope(pred$en, pred$y), cal_slope(pred$xgb, pred$y)),
  slope_200 = sapply(c("slope_lr", "slope_en", "slope_xgb"), function(v) q(runs[, v])[2]),
  slope_range = sapply(c("slope_lr", "slope_en", "slope_xgb"), function(v)
    paste(sprintf("%.2f", q(runs[, v])[c(1, 3)]), collapse = " to ")))
stopifnot(q(runs[, "slope_lr"])[3] < 1,                         # regression: too extreme in most runs
          q(runs[, "auc_xgb"])[2] < q(runs[, "auc_lr"])[2])
knitr::kable(counter, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Candidate", "AUC, 800 dev.", "AUC, 200 dev. (median)",
                           "Slope, 800 dev.", "Slope, 200 dev. (median)", "Slope, 10th to 90th percentile"),
             caption = "Counter-check: development on 25 random subsets of 200 instead of 800 synthetic patients; evaluation always on the same 400 test patients.")
```

With 200 development patients the subsets contain a median of `r q(runs[, "events"])[2]` events for eight
prespecified predictors. Discrimination drops only modestly for the regression models and somewhat more for boosting,
which has more to learn from fewer cases. The clearer change is in calibration. The unpenalised regression becomes
systematically overconfident: its median slope is `r sprintf("%.2f", counter$slope_200[1])` and stays below 1 in at
least 90% of the runs. The tuned models scatter in both directions, because the amount of shrinkage or the number of
boosting rounds is itself estimated from few events — sometimes too much, sometimes too little. This is why the sample
size of a prediction model is planned to limit overfitting and not only to estimate the AUC precisely
[@riley2020samplesize]. An AUC alone would have hidden the problem, which is the starting point of @sec-b06.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b05-consequences}

**Patients.** The model decides who is offered prevention, so its errors fall on people: a patient ranked below the
capacity line loses a chance of prevention. The points rule allocates care partly by age (85 or older), which needs a
clinical justification and a check of how it treats younger patients with other risk factors. Whether errors fall
unevenly on groups is a question for the test set, reported with denominators (@sec-b06, @sec-b21).

**Operations.** The rule needs three items the admitting clinician already knows; the regression eight values,
two of them laboratory results with missing values; the flexible models a reliable feed of 19 variables, a documented
imputation, a versioned model object and a plan for monitoring and updating (@sec-b20, @sec-b27). A gain of a few
cases per 400 patients has to be weighed against these costs and against a feed that fails silently.

**Regulation.** As soon as the output is used to allocate care to individual patients, the intended purpose of the
software has to be examined. If it qualifies as a medical device, Rule 11 in Annex VIII of the Medical Device
Regulation classifies software that provides information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic
purposes as class IIa or higher [@eu2017mdr]; the guidance of the Medical Device
Coordination Group [@mdcg2019-11] — guidance, not binding law — describes how qualification is assessed. Whether
an in-house pilot needs this assessment is a question for the local regulatory function (*open*; @sec-b22).

**Data protection and security.** Developing the model from routine data is a secondary use of health data and
needs its own legal basis and documentation (@sec-b23, @sec-b26). The stored model and its preprocessing statistics
are artefacts whose integrity has to be protected, because a changed median or coefficient changes every prediction
(@sec-b24).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b05-lookup}

**Reviewer question:** “Which data informed the preprocessing, which the tuning, which the choice of model family and
which the reported performance — and did any test patient contribute to the first three?” TRIPOD+AI asks authors to
describe how the data were partitioned and to specify all model-building steps, including hyperparameter tuning and
the method of internal validation [@collins2024tripodai, items 12a and 12c].

**Self-test:** A research group reports a random forest for delirium with an AUC of 0.86 from ten-fold
cross-validation on all 600 patients of their hospital. Before the cross-validation they selected the ten predictors
most strongly associated with delirium in the full data set. Which validation type is this, and what does the AUC of
0.86 estimate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is internal validation by cross-validation, but with predictor selection outside the resampling loop. The selection
has already seen the outcomes of every patient who is later held out, so the AUC of 0.86 is an optimistic estimate of
the performance of the whole procedure. A correct estimate would repeat the selection inside each training fold
(nested resampling) or confirm the final model on patients who played no part in development. Even then the result
would describe new patients from the same hospital and period, not another hospital.
:::

**Annotated sources:**

- @zou2005elasticnet introduces the elastic net, the penalty that mixes ridge and lasso and is tuned in Step 5.
- @friedman2010glmnet describes the coordinate-descent algorithm and parameterisation of glmnet used in the lab.
- @chen2016xgboost describes the gradient-boosting system behind the flexible candidate.
- @christodoulou2019mlvslr is the systematic review showing no average benefit of machine learning over logistic
  regression in comparisons at low risk of bias.
- @varma2006nestedcv shows that cross-validated error of a tuned classifier is biased and that nested
  cross-validation reduces the bias.
- @riley2020samplesize supports the counter-check: sample size for prediction models must limit overfitting, not only
  ensure precise performance estimates.
- @moons2025probastai and @collins2024tripodai provide the appraisal and reporting items cited for leakage, tuning
  and internal validation.
- @pedregosa2011sklearn is the reference for the scikit-learn implementation in the comparison box.
- The Medical Device Regulation [@eu2017mdr] and MDCG 2019-11 Rev. 1 [@mdcg2019-11] are the regulatory starting
  points for software that allocates care.
